strengths: Large-scale, systematically constructed benchmark (20,139 QA pairs) with real-world financial documents addressing genuine long-context evaluation gaps
Rigorous methodology with principled knowledge graph representation (RDF/SPARQL), structured annotation schema, and multi-round review under expert supervision
Comprehensive evaluation of 13 diverse models with multiple complementary metrics (F1, Edit Distance, Cosine Similarity, LLM-as-a-Judge) validated against human judgment (r=0.94-0.95)
Systematic complexity stratification along three interpretable dimensions (hops, set operations, plurality) enabling fine-grained difficulty analysis
Exceptional reproducibility: dev set released, code open-sourced, detailed annotation guidelines, prompting strategies documented, hardware specifications provided
Insightful error analysis with four categorized failure modes and clear performance degradation patterns (15% 'Not Found' at level 1 → 77% at level 5)
Honest handling of methodological limitations and explicit acknowledgment of scope constraints in discussion section
weaknesses: Critical omission of Inter-Annotator Agreement (IAA) metrics despite complex annotation schema and documented edge cases, undermining data quality claims and reproducibility
Narrow domain scope limited to SEC credit agreements; annotation schema (7 entity types specific to financial structures) is domain-dependent, making generalization claims speculative and unvalidated
Unjustified design choices: linear complexity metric (L=H+P+#SO) assumes equal weight across orthogonal dimensions; batch size of 50 questions arbitrary; temperature=0.0 unrealistic
Imbalanced dataset distribution (Easy: 32%, Hard: 3.5%) and poor fit between theoretical complexity and actual model performance (models sometimes perform better on medium than easy questions)
Counterintuitive finding unexplained: oracle passages outperform full documents on hard questions (Table 13), contradicting context-helps hypothesis without investigation
Limited baseline comparisons: no dense retrieval RAG, no fine-tuning experiments, weak implementation of retrieval baseline, no systematic ablation of model components
Inconsistent model evaluation with asterisked models evaluated on 'smaller subsets due to cost', compromising cross-model comparability and raising fairness concerns
Missing critical methodological details: SPARQL query generation process underspecified, how invalid templates are filtered unclear, gold standard answer quality unverified (test answers withheld)
Incremental insights: findings largely confirmatory (LLMs struggle with set operations and multi-hop reasoning already known from prior work), limited guidance for remediation

Evaluation methodology concerns: LLM-as-a-Judge uses Gemini-2.0-Pro introducing potential bias, merging strategy for multi-chunk documents vaguely described, human evaluation limited to 100 examples (0.5% of dataset)

Principled KG-based QA extraction using RDF/SPARQL enabling reproducibility and scalability

Shallow error analysis: only 4 anecdotal examples; categories (semantic misinterpretation, implicit gaps) are vague and circular; lacks systematic taxonomy, confusion matrices, or correlation with model properties; 'lost-in-the-middle' cited but not systematically tested
Limited data release: only 40/170 documents (23%) released; test set withheld; unclear actual repository locations; hampers reproducibility and future work
Missing comparisons: no direct evaluation on related financial QA benchmarks (DocFinQA, FinDVer); unclear whether this overlaps or complements existing work
Insufficient human evaluation: only 100/20,139 (0.5%) QA pairs; distribution across complexity levels not reported

Underspecified experimental choices: document sampling (17/year) appears arbitrary; question instance selection from templates not detailed; SPARQL entity selection process unclear; batch size (50) and chunk size (128K) not justified

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across 13 models with multiple metrics, human validation showing strong correlation (r≥0.94)
Large-scale, high-quality dataset of 20,139 QA pairs with ground truth extracted via SPARQL from knowledge graphs
Clear methodology with systematic annotation schema, well-documented edge cases, and reproducible QA generation pipeline
Insightful error analysis identifying four concrete failure modes (semantic misinterpretation, set operations, implicit information, retrieval)
Strong reproducibility: open-sourced code, detailed prompting strategies, comprehensive guidelines, planned leaderboard
Thorough appendices with annotation examples, full template specifications, and evaluation details
Practical significance using real-world SEC documents with high complexity and relevance

Small human evaluation sample (100/20,139 = 0.5%) without confidence intervals; correlation statistics lack error bars despite sample size limitations

strengths: Principled KG-based framework using RDF/SPARQL for deterministic, reproducible QA extraction from gold annotations

Comprehensive evaluation of 16 LLMs with four metrics validated against human judgment (Pearson r ≥ 0.94) and systematic error categorization
Strong reproducibility: 80.76% inter-annotator agreement, detailed annotation guidelines, prompting strategy, code/dataset release, clear methodology
Large-scale dataset (20,139 QA pairs from 170 real SEC documents) preserves natural document distribution without synthetic injection
Systematic error analysis identifying four recurring failure modes with quantitative trends and concrete examples

Counterintuitive Oracle<Full Document result for Hard questions (Table 17) suggests potential gold annotation issues or dataset quality problems requiring investigation
Limited domain generalizability: main dataset is SEC filings only; ablation study uses single 225-page medical document; framework requires significant domain expertise for new applications
Dataset imbalance: only 3.5% Hard questions (706/20,139); many Level 4-5 templates have <10 instances, limiting statistical power for difficult reasoning analysis

Narrow annotation schema (7 entity types) deliberately omits financial/contractual semantics without empirical validation of impact; design choice not rigorously justified

strengths: Systematic KG-based QA extraction with SPARQL templates ensures reproducibility and grounds questions in real document structure
Multi-dimensional complexity framework (hops × set operations × plurality) is more sophisticated than prior single-dimensional approaches
Comprehensive evaluation of 16 models with complementary metrics (F1, edit distance, cosine similarity, LLM-as-judge) and human validation
Extensive documentation with annotation guidelines, edge cases, ablations, and commitment to release data and code
Real documents from SEC EDGAR preserve authentic complexity absent in synthetic datasets
weaknesses: Severely limited to single domain (financial credit agreements only); medical ablation (1 document) does not demonstrate generalization
Shallow knowledge representation (7 entity types, 6 relations) captures only elementary relationships; real-world semantic complexity is lost
Significant chunking artifacts: performance drops 43% F1 with chunking (Table 14); two-stage merging is unnatural and undermines 'long-context' evaluation claims
Circular ground truth: questions generated from annotations, which themselves required subjective interpretation; difficult to assess if model disagreements are errors or reasonable alternatives
Set operations analysis is superficial—involves only 2-3 items; unclear whether failures stem from logical reasoning or basic entity tracking
Evaluation metrics problematic: LLM-as-judge bias (using Gemini-2.0-Pro), brittleness of F1 on short answers, treatment of 'Not Found' as always wrong, human evaluation on only 100 questions
Limited novelty: combines known components (KGs, templates, LLM eval); incremental over MuSiQue's template-based approach
Severely imbalanced dataset: only 3.5% hard questions; authors acknowledge highly complex templates 'often become inapplicable to real documents'
Descriptive rather than explanatory error analysis: categorizes failures but doesn't investigate root causes or model-level patterns
RAG baseline comparison (Table 17) superficial—poor performance may reflect setup rather than fundamental unsuitability

strengths: Novel three-dimensional complexity framework (hops, set operations, plurality) provides fine-grained control over question difficulty—more systematic than prior work
Rigorous dataset construction: 80.76% IAA, comprehensive annotation guidelines addressing edge cases, RDF/SPARQL-based systematic extraction eliminates manual authoring biases
Thorough evaluation of 16 models with multiple metrics validated against human judgment (r=0.941 F1, r=0.947 LLM-J correlation with humans)
Clear error analysis identifying four failure modes with concrete examples; oracle vs. full-document comparison (D.8) reveals importance of implicit context for complex reasoning
Strong reproducibility: partial dataset release (40/170 docs), code and inference pipeline released, leaderboard setup, cross-domain ablation demonstrates generalizability
Well-justified domain selection; credit agreements have rich entity structures and real-world significance for long-context evaluation
weaknesses: Domain-specific dataset (credit agreements only) with limited cross-domain validation—ablation on medical documents is minimal (one 225-page document); unclear how framework applies to different structured domains

Severely imbalanced hard questions: only 706 hard (L=5) questions out of 20,139 total (3.5%); human performance surprisingly high on hard questions (F1=0.935, Table 16) suggests these may not be genuinely complex

Complexity measure L=H+P+#SO is ad-hoc and unjustified: no empirical evidence that additive combination captures difficulty; set operations vary inherently but weighted equally; boundary between Medium/Hard appears arbitrary

Limited template coverage with skewed distribution: many templates have <10 instances at higher complexity levels; authors acknowledge highly compositional templates become inapplicable to real documents, limiting scalability claims

Cross-model analysis is aggregate; no investigation of which models exhibit which failure modes (e.g., do reasoning-focused models handle implicit information better?) limiting insights for model development

Evaluation uses uniform 128K token chunking strategy for all models despite some supporting longer contexts, creating artificial 'lost-in-the-middle' effects; stratified sampling for cost-constrained models means non-uniform evaluation
Set operations receive shallow treatment despite being a key contribution: only aggregate analysis; no breakdown by operation type (∩, ¬, ∪); limited investigation of why models fail at Boolean logic
Data contamination risk not discussed: SEC EDGAR documents are public and likely in training data; no contamination screening mentioned for leaderboard
